strengths: Elegant and technically well-motivated core idea: extending RoPE to a set of discrete reference frames drawn from Platonic solid symmetry groups, yielding combined translation and roto-reflection equivariance while preserving the exact computation graph and cost of a standard Transformer.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper provides a careful group-theoretic derivation of RoPE (Appendix A), formal equivariance proofs (Appendix C), and a novel and interesting formal connection between linear RoPE-attention and dynamic (group) convolution with linear-time complexity (Prop. 2, Corollary 1).

Broad and diverse empirical validation spanning 2D vision (CIFAR-10), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and molecular property prediction (QM9, OMol25), testing both 'equivariant' and 'non-equivariant' task regimes.

Practical efficiency story is compelling: parameter count reduction via weight-sharing (e.g., CIFAR-10 84M vs 21M params with better accuracy), competitive inference times versus TFN/G-Hyena, and a promising Fourier-domain implementation (Appendix M) showing further scalability at larger hidden dimensions.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset descriptions, and (per the reproducibility statement) attached source code with plans to open-source.
weaknesses: The claimed equivariance is only to a finite discrete subgroup (12/24/60 elements) rather than full continuous SO(3)/O(3); the paper's repeated framing as 'approximately SE(n)/E(n)-equivariant' is somewhat imprecise and the practical consequences of this approximation (e.g., generalization to arbitrary unseen rotations) are not rigorously quantified.

Some central experimental comparisons are inconclusive or self-undermining: the QM9 comparison to EquiformerV2 shows near-parity rather than a clear win; the OMol25 comparison is only favorable under an artificially matched compute budget, while literature-reported numbers with more compute show a large gap (e.g., force MAE 10.11 vs 24.25), and the 'we leave this for future work' framing understates this limitation.

The key design choice of using constant keys (kj=1) to avoid training instability on QM9/OMol25 is justified only by post-hoc narrative/hypothesis, without a controlled ablation or quantitative evidence (e.g., loss curves) demonstrating the claimed instability of the mixed-kernel formulation.
Appendix B ('Related Works') is essentially an unfinished placeholder (a bare list of method names with no discussion), which is a significant presentation lapse.

The PCA-frame variant (Table 3, '8-Refl + 1 frame') performs far worse than the paper's own end-to-end attention models (0.039 vs 0.010 MAE), yet is used to claim superiority over Frame Averaging baselines (FAFormer); this comparison is somewhat confusing and could be presented more carefully.
Reported wall-clock timings have implausibly large variance (e.g., 2.01 ± 3.74 ms for the standard Transformer), raising questions about the reliability/rigor of the timing methodology.

Guidance on how to select the appropriate Platonic group for a new task/domain is limited; the paper relies on extensive per-task hyperparameter sweeps rather than offering principled selection criteria, which may hinder practical adoption.

The core equivariant machinery (group convolutions, weight-sharing via Schur's lemma decomposition) draws heavily on well-established group-equivariant network theory; the primary novelty is its specific combination with RoPE-attention, which, while useful, is an incremental (though valuable) conceptual step rather than a fundamentally new theoretical framework.

strengths: The core technical idea is elegant: reinterpreting RoPE-based attention as operating over a set of Platonic-solid reference frames yields a principled weight-sharing scheme that achieves approximate E(n) equivariance while leaving the standard Transformer computation graph and cost completely unchanged. This is a genuinely appealing resolution of the symmetry-vs-scalability trade-off.

The formal connection between softmax-free RoPE attention and dynamic (group) convolution (Prop. 2, Cor. 1) is a nice theoretical contribution that also yields a practical linear-time variant, and the group-theoretic derivations (Appendices A, C-E, M) are carried out carefully with proofs.

Experiments span a genuinely diverse set of domains (2D vision, 3D point clouds, small-molecule and large-scale molecular property/force prediction), and the paper includes comparisons to relevant recent baselines (EquiformerV2, FAFormer, G-Hyena, TFN, eSEN).

The reproducibility effort is substantial: code is included, extensive hyperparameter tables and dataset/training details are given in the appendix, and a hyperparameter-tuning protocol is described to ensure fair compute-matched comparisons between T(n) and SE(n) variants.
The Fourier-domain implementation analysis (Appendix M) is a thoughtful additional contribution showing a path to further efficiency gains as hidden dimension grows.
weaknesses: Several central quantitative claims are less convincing on close inspection: on QM9 the proposed model is beaten by Rapidash (alpha MAE 0.040 vs. 0.048), yet the text still frames the results as delivering results 'on par with state-of-the-art'; on OMol25, the paper's own literature numbers show eSEN trained with ~4x more compute achieves dramatically better accuracy (Force 10.11 vs. 24.25, Energy 29.80 vs. 74.00) than the proposed model, and the favorable comparison is only against the authors' own compute-constrained reproduction of eSEN, which is a fairly narrow and potentially cherry-picked basis for the paper's significance claims.

Main results tables (Tables 1, 2, 3, 5) report only single numbers with no variance/seed information, despite the differences between groups/configurations (e.g., CIFAR-10 C4 vs C6 vs D4 vs D6, 92.73 vs 92.16 vs 92.53 vs 92.07) being small enough that statistical significance is unclear; only the inference-timing table (Table 4) includes error bars.

The claimed gains from incorporating symmetry are inconsistent and not obviously monotonic in group size (e.g., on CIFAR-10, C6 underperforms C4 despite more reference frames), which weakens the paper's central narrative that more symmetry structure reliably helps, and this non-monotonicity is not discussed or explained.

The Related Works section (Appendix B) is left essentially as an unfinished list of paper titles with no citations or discussion ('Equivariant Transformers. SE(3) Transformer, EFA, G-Hyena, EScAIP, GATr'), which is a significant presentation lapse for a submitted manuscript and undermines confidence in the overall polish/rigor of the submission.

The key experimental claim motivating the constant-key ('purely geometric') kernel design choice—that learned/mixed keys cause severe training instability on QM9/OMol25—is asserted only qualitatively, without any supporting loss curves, quantitative instability metrics, or ablation numbers to substantiate it.

The 'full' E(n)/SE(n) equivariance claims are only exact with respect to the small discrete Platonic subgroups (12–60 elements) rather than the continuous rotation group, and in 3D only rotational subgroups are used (reflections excluded for tractability); this approximate nature is acknowledged but the framing in the abstract/title ('Solid Choice for Equivariance', 'Platonic ideal') somewhat oversells the achieved equivariance relative to what is actually guaranteed.

The higher-performing full-attention variant remains quadratic in sequence length, and the truly linear-time convolutional variant consistently underperforms attention by a non-trivial margin across all reported benchmarks (e.g., ~4 points on CIFAR-10, ~1.5 points on ScanObjectNN), so the headline 'no additional cost, at no scaling penalty' story is really only fully realized by the weaker of the two proposed variants.

strengths: The core theoretical contribution is elegant and well-motivated: reframing RoPE attention through group representation theory and extending it to full Euclidean equivariance via parallel per-frame attention heads defined by Platonic solid symmetry groups. This preserves the exact computation graph and cost of a standard Transformer, which is a genuinely valuable practical property that distinguishes this work from prior equivariant-attention methods that require costly architectural changes.

The formal connection between softmax-free RoPE attention and dynamic (group) convolution (Prop. 2, Cor. 1) is a nice theoretical result that yields a practically useful linear-time variant, and the authors provide full proofs in the appendix.

The experimental scope is broad, spanning 2D vision (CIFAR-10), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and molecular property prediction at both small (QM9) and large scale (OMol25), which helps demonstrate the general applicability of the framework.

Ablations comparing trivial vs. Platonic groups, attention vs. convolutional variants, and invariant vs. equivariant attention scores are informative and support the core claims about the benefit of the geometric inductive bias.
Reproducibility efforts are reasonably strong: detailed hyperparameter tables, an explicit description of the tuning protocol (Appendix H), and code attached as supplementary material.

The exploration of a Fourier-domain implementation (Appendix M) is a thoughtful additional contribution that points to a promising direction for scaling the method further, and the authors are transparent that it is not yet a mature optimization.
weaknesses: On QM9, the paper's own attention-based Platonic Transformer is only on par with (not better than) EquiformerV2 on the reported metric (mu), and its convolutional variant is notably worse than Rapidash (0.012 vs 0.010 on mu, 0.047 vs 0.040 on alpha), yet the framing in the text emphasizes competitiveness without fully acknowledging these gaps. Also, only 2 of the standard 12+ QM9 targets are reported, limiting the strength of the evidence.

The OMol25 comparison uses a highly constrained, non-standard compute budget (120 GPU-hours vs. the 475 GPU-hours estimated for literature eSEN), and the paper's own reproduced eSEN baseline under this budget performs far worse than literature-reported eSEN (e.g., force MAE 23.92 vs. 10.11). This large discrepancy raises questions about whether the reproduced baseline is well-tuned/representative, and the claimed 'outperforms eSEN' result should be interpreted cautiously given this gap to true SOTA is not closed nor clearly contextualized.

The hypothesis about mixed vs. purely geometric kernels causing training instability on QM9/OMol25 (Remark 1 / Section 4.1) is presented as an explanation but is not rigorously ablated or quantitatively substantiated—it reads as post-hoc reasoning rather than a validated empirical finding.

Appendix B ('Related Works') is essentially a bare list of method names under two headings with no discussion, comparison, or citations—this appears unfinished and is a notable presentation gap for a paper otherwise careful about related work in the main text.

The method only achieves equivariance to a discretized/finite subgroup of SO(3)/O(3) (Platonic solid symmetries), not exact continuous rotational equivariance; the paper is reasonably upfront about this design choice, but the practical implications (how much approximation error this introduces for continuous-symmetry tasks) are not empirically quantified.

Selecting the appropriate Platonic group (tetrahedron vs. octahedron vs. cyclic/dihedral, etc.) for a given task requires hyperparameter search rather than a principled default, adding practical overhead not fully discussed as a limitation.

The 'at no additional cost' framing, while largely true for the FLOP/parameter-matched comparisons, relies on a specific head-count matching convention (Appendix H) that is somewhat indirect; broader wall-clock evidence is limited to a small set of QM9 batch timings.

strengths: Elegant and well-motivated core idea: defining RoPE-attention relative to a set of reference frames drawn from Platonic solid symmetry groups yields combined translation + discrete roto-reflection equivariance while leaving the attention mechanism, computation graph, and cost of a standard Transformer completely unchanged. This directly resolves the long-standing scalability vs. symmetry-awareness trade-off in a principled way.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper provides formal proofs (Appendix A-C) that ground RoPE in group representation theory, prove end-to-end equivariance of the architecture, and establish a rigorous equivalence between linear RoPE-attention and a dynamic, content-aware group convolution with linear-time complexity (Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.3).

Broad and diverse experimental validation across vision (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and multiple molecular tasks (QM9 regression and generation, OMol25 property/force prediction, ProteinMD), with the method matching or outperforming specialized state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., outperforming eSEN-sm on OMol25 with 2.6x higher throughput, outperforming G-Hyena on ProteinMD).

Thorough ablation studies, including group-size effects, equivariant vs. invariant attention scores, fixed vs. learned key trade-offs with an optimization-sensitivity analysis (Appendix M), equivariance-error measurements before/after training, and a forward-looking exploration of Fourier-domain implementations that show further throughput gains at larger hidden dimensions.

High degree of reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter tables for every dataset, explicit training protocols, and runtime/timing benchmarks against reference equivariant architectures (G-Hyena, TFN), lending credibility to the practical efficiency claims.
weaknesses: The method only guarantees equivariance to discrete subgroups of O(n) (Platonic solids/polygon symmetries), not full continuous SE(3)/E(3) equivariance; this is acknowledged but somewhat undercuts the generality suggested by framing (e.g., 'approximate E(n) equivariance'), and the practical difference from full continuous equivariance is not deeply quantified beyond one QM9 equivariance-error table.

Some equivariant-task results show only modest improvements (e.g., the validity gap between DiP-{e} and DiP-Tetrahedron on QM9 generation is small), and the paper's own discussion suggests Transformers may already partially learn approximate equivariance without the constraint, which slightly weakens the centrality of the claimed inductive-bias benefit at scale.

The OMol25 comparison relies on a single external baseline (eSEN-sm, 6M params) that is considerably smaller than the proposed 60M-parameter models; a more extensive comparison against other scalable MLIP architectures at matched parameter/compute budgets would strengthen the scalability claims.

Several large-scale results (e.g., OMol25 Table 5) appear to be single runs without reported variance/seeds, unlike the CIFAR-10/ScanObjectNN tables, making it harder to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains.

The Fourier-domain implementation, while promising, is presented as a preliminary/unoptimized proof-of-concept relegated to the appendix and not integrated into the main experimental pipeline, so the practical efficiency benefits of the 'linear-time convolutional variant' and Fourier speedups are only partially demonstrated in the main results.

The paper is notation-heavy and assumes substantial familiarity with group representation theory (irreps, Schur's lemma, Cayley tables), which may limit accessibility to a broader ICML audience despite the otherwise clear high-level narrative.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely elegant mechanism: defining attention relative to discrete Platonic-solid reference frames so that equivariance can be induced purely through weight-sharing, without altering the attention computation graph or FLOP count of a standard Transformer+RoPE. This is a nontrivial and reasonably novel way to inject geometric inductive bias into Transformers.

The formal connection between linear (softmax-free) RoPE attention and dynamic/group convolution (Prop 4.1, Cor 4.3) is a clean theoretical contribution that gives a principled interpretation of RoPE as a content-adaptive geometric filter, and yields a legitimate linear-time alternative.

The experimental scope is broad and spans heterogeneous domains (2D vision, 3D point clouds, molecular property prediction, molecular dynamics, molecule generation, large-scale interatomic potentials), with consistent ablations (group choice, fixed vs. learned keys, invariant vs equivariant scores, Fourier-domain implementation) that probe the method from multiple angles.

The appendices are unusually thorough: full proofs, equivariance-error measurements, attention visualizations, and an honest discussion of optimization sensitivity of learned keys (Appendix M), which adds credibility and reproducibility value.
The limitations section is forthright about only guaranteeing equivariance to discrete subgroups of O(n) rather than full continuous groups, and about untested extreme-scale behavior.
weaknesses: The central marketing claim of 'equivariance at no additional cost' is more nuanced than advertised: matching FLOPs/heads across configurations entails large reductions in parameter count (e.g., Table 1: 14.2M vs 85.1M; Table 5: Octahedron-30M underperforms Tetrahedron-60M, attributed to capacity loss rather than group size). This conflates 'same compute graph' with 'no cost,' and makes head-to-head comparisons harder to interpret cleanly, since capacity confounds group-size effects.

The equivariance obtained is only to finite discrete subgroups of O(3)/O(2) (orders up to 60), not full continuous rotation groups, yet the paper's title and framing ('A Solid Choice for Equivariance,' 'achieves E(n) equivariance') can overstate what is actually guaranteed; the measured non-zero equivariance error after training (Appendix N.1) underscores that this is an approximation rather than exact equivariance.

Empirical results are mixed rather than consistently state-of-the-art: on QM9 property prediction (Table 10) the model trails specialized architectures (PaiNN, TorchMD-NET, SphereNet) on several targets, and the paper explicitly disclaims pursuing SOTA, which weakens the significance claims relative to the strong rhetorical framing in the abstract/intro.

Some comparisons use baselines with substantially different parameter budgets (e.g., OMol25: eSEN-sm at 6M vs. Platonic Transformer at 60M params), which complicates attributing throughput/accuracy gains specifically to the proposed equivariance mechanism rather than to scale.

The theoretically appealing linear-time convolutional variant (no softmax, constant/fixed keys) shows a consistent and non-trivial accuracy drop versus full attention (~5-6 points on CIFAR-10/ScanObjectNN), limiting its practical utility beyond a conceptual scalability argument.

The learned-key attention variant is shown to be optimization-sensitive and prone to divergence without extra stabilization (QK-norm, high weight decay), as documented in Appendix M; this fragility is relegated to the appendix and not prominently flagged as a limitation of the core attention design in the main text.

The hyperparameter tuning protocol differs across tasks (comprehensive sweep for CIFAR-10/ScanObjectNN vs. a sequential QM9-to-OMol25 transfer procedure), which could introduce inconsistent advantages across benchmarks and makes cross-task comparisons less controlled.

The explanation for why equivariance helps on 'non-equivariant' tasks (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN) is largely post-hoc and speculative ('may act as a regularizer'), without a rigorous mechanistic analysis.

strengths: Elegant and well-motivated core idea: defining attention relative to Platonic-solid reference frames combined with (unmodified) RoPE yields roto-translation equivariance while leaving the attention computation graph, FLOP count, and architecture of a standard Transformer completely unchanged -- directly resolving the long-standing scalability vs. symmetry trade-off.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper provides clean derivations (grounded in representation/Fourier theory, Appendix A) showing RoPE is itself a translation-equivariant irrep construction, formal equivariance proofs for the full architecture (Appendix B), and a novel, rigorously proved connection between (linear) RoPE attention and dynamic/group convolution with linear-time complexity (Props 4.1, Cor 4.3).

Very broad and convincing empirical validation spanning vision (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and multiple molecular tasks (QM9 regression and generation, OMol25 force/energy prediction, ProteinMD), with the model matching or beating specialized domain SOTA (e.g., outperforming eSEN-sm on OMol25 with 2.6x higher throughput, beating G-Hyena on ProteinMD).

Extensive and thoughtful ablations in the appendix: group-size vs. head-count trade-offs, equivariant vs. invariant attention scores, fixed vs. learned key stability analysis (with weight-decay/QK-norm mitigation), equivariance-error measurements before/after training, attention visualization, and a promising Fourier-domain implementation analysis showing further efficiency gains at scale.

Good reproducibility support: detailed architecture and hyperparameter tables (Table 12) and dataset/training protocols are provided for every experiment, and the method is framed as a simple structural constraint on existing modules rather than a new complex module, aiding implementation.
weaknesses: The method only yields equivariance to a finite/discrete subgroup of O(n) (Platonic solid symmetries) rather than full continuous SO(3)/O(3) equivariance; this approximation is acknowledged but its practical consequences (e.g., residual equivariance error under arbitrary rotations) are only briefly explored (Appendix N.1) rather than being a central, carefully characterized part of the evaluation.

Some comparisons for non-equivariant tasks are not fully capacity-controlled: e.g., in Table 1 the trivial/{e} CIFAR-10 baseline has 85.1M parameters versus 14.2-21.3M for symmetry-group variants; while this parameter reduction is an intended consequence of weight-sharing, it complicates isolating whether gains stem from the inductive bias itself or from the resulting regularization/implicit capacity control, especially since no larger-capacity (matched-parameter) baseline is swept to rule out underfitting of the {e} model.

The design choices around fixed vs. learned key vectors (Section 4.1/Remark 4.2 and Appendix M) are justified with a largely narrative, post-hoc explanation (geometry vs. statistical-correlation tasks) rather than a more principled or predictive account of when each choice should be preferred; the optimization sensitivity of learned keys without QK-norm also suggests some fragility in the proposed mixed-kernel variant.

Large-scale validation is somewhat limited: OMol25 experiments use the 4M subset (out of >100M available structures) and at most 80 epochs, so claims of scalability to truly large regimes remain only partially demonstrated, as also acknowledged in the Limitations section.

The throughput/efficiency claim of 'no additional cost' is nuanced in practice: the Fourier-domain analysis (Appendix O) shows that a naive spatial implementation is actually less efficient than standard Transformers at larger hidden dimensions unless a more complex Fourier-domain implementation is used, indicating the strict zero-overhead claim holds cleanly only in specific regimes.
